script: [serious] A year before Apollo 1, an engineer warned NASA: the first fire in a spacecraft may well be fatal. He was right. January 27th, 1967. Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee were strapped into their capsule on the launch pad for a routine test. Nobody thought it was dangerous. The rocket wasn't even fueled. But the cabin was filled with pure oxygen, pressurized above the air outside. The contractor's engineers had wanted a safer mix of gases. NASA chose pure oxygen. The materials inside had been fire-tested at a much lower pressure. And flammable Velcro and nylon netting had piled up in the cabin. That afternoon, a wire under the crew's feet sparked. Then Grissom's voice on the radio. We've got a fire in the cockpit. In pure oxygen, the fire filled the capsule in seconds. The hatch opened inward, and the pressure held it shut. Even on a good day, it took over forty seconds to open. All three astronauts were killed. NASA rebuilt the capsule. A hatch that opened outward in seconds. Fire-resistant materials. No more pure oxygen on the pad. Twenty-one months later, Apollo 7 flew. Send this to someone who thinks safety rules are written for no reason. This is Dossier Decoded. Case file number forty-two. A new file every day.
